---
title: "Signals: Values with Addresses"
---

The values $1,2,2,5$ can describe four die throws. They can also describe measurements at four places.

The numbers alone do not tell us which arrangement we have. Their addresses provide the missing structure.

## 🔰 A signal assigns values to addresses {#sec-sample-signals-a-signal-assigns-values-to-addresses}

Write

$$
S:\mathbb T\longrightarrow\mathcal V,
\qquad t\longmapsto S[t].
$$

Read this aloud: **at an address $t$ in the domain $\mathbb T$, the signal supplies a value of type $\mathcal V$.**

The notation $S[t]$ keeps the notes' idea of evaluation. We ask at an address; we receive a value.

For four throws,

$$
\mathbb T=\{1,2,3,4\},
\qquad
S[1]=1,\ S[2]=2,\ S[3]=2,\ S[4]=5.
$$

The domain describes the places where questions are allowed. The value type describes the answers that make sense.

## 🏵 The address supplies relationships {#sec-sample-signals-the-address-supplies-relationships}

Time carries an order and measurable intervals. A pixel grid supplies neighbors in two dimensions. A list of patient identifiers supplies identity, but its numbering need not describe distance or order in any medically meaningful sense.

Operations must respect that difference.

Subtracting successive voltages can describe change over time. Subtracting the ages of patient 103 and patient 104 does not become a time derivative because the identifiers happen to be consecutive.

The structure of $\mathbb T$ is part of the signal.

## ⚙️ Alignment comes before arithmetic {#sec-sample-signals-alignment-comes-before-arithmetic}

Suppose two sensors observe the same room:

$$
A[\text{noon}]=20,\qquad
B[\text{noon}]=21.
$$

Their difference at noon is meaningful if their units and calibration are comparable.

If row one of one file means noon and row one of another means midnight, subtracting the rows silently creates a different experiment. Equal array lengths do not establish matching addresses.

A combined observation can instead preserve both readings:

$$
C[t]=(A[t],B[t]).
$$

Its value type is now a pair. We have changed the kind of answer without changing the address domain.

## 💡 Order is information we may choose to lose {#sec-sample-signals-order-is-information-we-may-choose-to-lose}

Consider

$$
S=(1,2,2,5),
\qquad
R=(2,5,1,2).
$$

They contain the same values with the same multiplicities. Their temporal behavior differs. One rises; the other rises, falls, and rises again.

Sorting preserves the collection of values while replacing observation order with rank. A histogram goes further: it retains how often each value occurred.

For a process with memory, those transformations can remove the evidence that reveals the memory.

## ☯ A profile is also a signal {#sec-sample-signals-a-profile-is-also-a-signal}

The notation can describe more than a record through time.

A potential profile $P[f]$ assigns a weight to each possible value $f$. Its addresses are values, and its outputs are weights. The original record $S[t]$ instead assigns an observed value to each observation address.

The same architecture supports both:

- $S[t]$: observation address $\to$ observed value.
- $P[f]$: possible value $\to$ potential weight.

Keeping their domains visible prevents us from summing over observations when we intended to sum over possibilities.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try the idea {#sec-sample-signals-try-the-idea}

Two files each contain 24 temperatures. Is their element-by-element difference automatically meaningful? What must be checked first?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Work it through {#sec-sample-signals-work-it-through}

Check which times and locations the rows represent, whether the units agree, and how the measurements were obtained. Twenty-four rows establish a count. They do not establish alignment.
